title: Peace in the home
hook: a high value in Jewish family life

segments.voice: Yesterday's line was communities differ: these and these, argued honestly, with each side taught fairly. Whose view did you state well? Today, the smallest community there is: one home. Day one thousand three hundred eleven.

Sarah is inside the tent, listening. Outside, a guest tells Abraham that by this time next year, Sarah will have a son. She laughs to herself. In the King James words, she says: "After I am waxed old shall I have pleasure, my lord being old also?" A verse later, God speaks to Abraham about that laugh, and repeats what she said. Except the repeat is different. Listen closely to it, because the whole of today's word hides in the part that goes missing.
screen: `SARAH LAUGHS IN THE TENT.` → `"MY LORD BEING OLD ALSO."` → `GOD REPEATS IT, DIFFERENTLY.`

segments.voice: Shalom bayit. Peace in the home. Turn it four ways. First, the missing words. When God tells Abraham what Sarah said, the King James has it as: "Shall I of a surety bear a child, which am old?" Sarah's age stays in. Abraham's age is gone. Sarah had said, my lord is old too. God reports only that she said, I am old. The Talmud notices the change and draws a lesson from it: great is peace, for even the Holy One altered words for its sake. Third parties don't need to carry every sharp word from one spouse to the other. Second, peace is something you chase. Hillel taught: be among the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace. Pursuing. Peace at home doesn't arrive on its own; somebody goes after it. Tradition tells of Aaron going to each side of a quarrel separately, telling each how much the other regretted it, until they met and embraced. Third, it's small and daily. The Talmud asks: if someone can afford only one light, for Shabbat or for Hanukkah, which comes first? The Shabbat lamp in the home, it answers, for the sake of shalom bayit. A lit house, where nobody trips in the dark and tempers don't flare. Peace, in this teaching, starts with something as plain as being able to see each other. Fourth, what it isn't. Shalom bayit is not silence, and it's not keeping up appearances. Teachers of this value say clearly that it never asks anyone to stay where they are not safe. It means a home where people are gentle on purpose, choose their words with care, and keep making the first move toward each other.
screen: `THE WORDS GOD LEFT OUT.` · `LOVING PEACE, PURSUING PEACE.` · `A LAMP SO WE CAN SEE.` · `NOT SILENCE, NOT DANGER.` · then, large: `PEACE AT HOME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make one small peace at home. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the people you live with, or the people closest to you if you live alone. Is there one small friction between you right now: a sharp word, a chore, a silence that's gone on a little long? Don't try to fix the whole thing. Choose one small move toward peace: a kind word, a task done without being asked, a sharp sentence you decide not to pass along. Hold that one move until it feels doable today. The bell holds the time.
Shalom bayit: peace in the home. Pursued, not waited for, and built from small choices, like the words God left out for Sarah and Abraham. Today's word.
Your line: peace at home. Today, make the first small move toward someone you live with, before they make it. Day one thousand three hundred eleven.

howItsDone: Jewish tradition counts shalom bayit, peace in the home, as a high value in family life; teachers draw on texts like God's softened report of Sarah's words and Hillel's call to love and pursue peace.

myth: God repeats Sarah's words to Abraham word for word
the part about Abraham's age is left out, and the Talmud says it was for peace.
the Talmud puts the Shabbat lamp before Hanukkah lights, for peace at home
if you can afford only one, the home's Shabbat light comes first.
shalom bayit means staying quiet about everything
it's not silence, and it never asks anyone to stay where they aren't safe.

fork.setup: Sarah laughed and said she was old, and that Abraham was old too. you're about to tell Abraham what she said. what do you say?
options: repeat every word, including the part about his age.
say only that she laughed because she is old.
tell him nothing about the laugh.
fork.reveal: God reports only Sarah's own age; the Talmud learns from this that even the Holy One altered words for the sake of peace.

original.note: Hebrew: peace of the house, peace in the home.

trapdoor: what you thought: shalom bayit just means no fighting at home.
what it means: pursuing peace with the people you live with, through small daily choices.
what a scholar hears: Yevamot 65b on Genesis 18:12–13, Shabbat 23b's lamp, and Hillel's "loving peace and pursuing peace" in Avot 1:12.

sources.quoted: After I am waxed old shall I have pleasure, my lord being old also?
Shall I of a surety bear a child, which am old?

notes: Genesis 18:12–13 quoted from the KJV; confirm wording. 'By this time next year' paraphrases Genesis 18:10 ('according to the time of life').
Yevamot 65b (also Bava Metzia 87a): 'great is peace, for even the Holy One altered [words] for its sake', learned from Genesis 18:12–13. Paraphrased; confirm.

Avot 1:12 (Hillel: be of the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace) paraphrased; Aaron making peace between quarreling parties from Avot de-Rabbi Natan 12, introduced as 'tradition tells'. Confirm.
Shabbat 23b: Shabbat lamp takes precedence over Hanukkah lamp because of shalom bayit. Confirm. 'Nobody trips in the dark and tempers don't flare' is an explanatory gloss (cf. Rashi); confirm.

Safety line: 'Teachers of this value say clearly that it never asks anyone to stay where they are not safe.' Included deliberately because shalom bayit has been misused to pressure people to stay in abusive homes; confirm the wording with a Keeper.
